unit.title: Plan for wiring and installation of electrical/electronic machinery appliances and fixtures

summary: This unit teaches you to plan the wiring of fixed appliances, machines and fixtures before work starts: reading the maker's instructions and nameplate, surveying the site, working out currents, choosing circuits, protection, isolators and cables, allowing for the place and its environment, planning fixings, writing the method statement and risk assessment, sequencing the work with other trades, and planning tests and handover.

blocks.p: Water heaters, stoves, A/C units, pumps, gate motors, ceiling fans, light fittings and electronic equipment all need a circuit, protection, a way to switch them off, and a safe fixing. At Level 3 you **plan** that work: you decide what is needed, in what order, with what, and how it will be done safely, before anyone picks up a drill. A good plan means the installer can work without guessing, and the client gets an appliance that works safely for years.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read the maker's installation instructions, nameplate and wiring diagram; survey the site, the supply, the board and the route.
Find the current of each appliance and check the supply and board can carry the total.
Choose the supply voltage, own circuits, 2-pole or single-pole breakers, GFCI (RCD) protection and local isolators.
Pick cable size from the current, correction factors and volt drop; choose a safe route.
Outdoors, bathrooms, kitchens, hot roof spaces, damp and sea air.
Fixings for the weight and movement; clearances; fixtures such as fans and recessed lights.
Surge protection, dedicated circuits, earthing and anti-static handling.
Write the method statement and risk assessment
Steps in order, safe isolation, hazards and controls, people and tools.
Order the work and agree positions with the client, A/C installer, plumber, kitchen fitter and painter.
Plan the tests, handover and cost
Dead tests before energising; documents and circuit chart; labour hours, materials and approval.

blocks.note: You plan; you do not guess. Every figure in your plan comes from the nameplate, the maker's instructions, a table the Centre gives, or a calculation you can show. Where the maker's instructions and your habit differ, the maker's instructions win.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Homes and small businesses have a 50 Hz **110/220 V split-phase** supply. Lights, outlets and small appliances run at 110 V; water heaters, stoves, A/C units and many pumps run at 220 V from **two line conductors**. Larger buildings may have three-phase.

head: Source
What it tells you
rows: Supply voltage, circuit and protection needs, cable size, clearances, fixing, isolator position, special conditions. **The first document to read.**
Voltage, power (W or kW) or current (A), frequency, sometimes minimum cable and maximum breaker ratings (MCA and MOP) and the IP rating.
How the appliance's terminals, controls, motor and sensors are connected, for example a gate motor's controller.
Positions, circuit numbers, cable types, workmanship.
Care, servicing and what voids the warranty.

blocks.p: A plumber's invoice, a shop receipt or the old heater's warranty card does not give the new heater's supply, protection and clearances. Colour, model year, serial number, the country of manufacture and the size of the carton are not used to size a circuit.
Visit before you finish the plan. Check:

head: Item
What to record
rows: 110/220 V available; main breaker size; the existing load. A large appliance may be more than the main supply can carry.
Spare ways, condition, earthing, circuit chart. No spare way: plan a larger or extra board, agreed with the client.
Type, age, damage, signs of faults, to be reported.
Length from board to appliance; walls, ceilings, hot or wet areas, other services; hidden pipes and cables.
Agreed with the client and the installer (for example the A/C installer for indoor and outdoor units); wall or ceiling strong enough; clearances the maker asks for.
Outdoors, bathroom, kitchen, hot roof space; work at height; dust; the client's belongings.

blocks.note: Do not open a live board on the survey. Look, measure and record. A board that must be opened is opened by an authorised person with the circuits isolated.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Do not connect an appliance to the wrong supply

blocks.p: If the client buys a 220 V stove but the house has only 110 V, the planner explains that a 220 V supply is needed and plans it with JPS. Do not connect it to 110 V 'to see if it works', do not join two 110 V outlets to make 220 V, and do not fit a smaller fuse inside the stove. A 110–120 V appliance on a 220 V supply gets twice its rated voltage and can burn out or start a fire.

Use the nameplate current. If only power is given: **current = power ÷ voltage** (for resistive loads such as heaters and cookers; for motors use the nameplate current, which includes power factor and efficiency).

head: Appliance
Working
Current
rows: Six LED lights of 18 W, 110 V
Kettle 1 650 W + microwave 1 100 W together, 110 V

blocks.p: Units: 1 kW = 1 000 W, so a 0.75 kW motor is 750 W.

Before adding a large appliance, compare the new total with the **main breaker, main cable and service**. If the main supply cannot carry the extra, a service upgrade must be planned with JPS. Never fit a bigger main breaker than the cable allows.

Large loads such as A/C units, stoves, water heaters and many pumps are supplied at **220 V** because they then draw about **half the current** of the same power at 110 V, so the cable can be smaller and the volt drop lower. Small loads such as lights, fans and outlets use 110 V.

ul: A water heater, stove, A/C unit or pump normally has **its own circuit**: its big load could overload a shared circuit, and it can be isolated without losing anything else.
If two appliances used together would draw more than a circuit's breaker allows, they go on **separate circuits**: do not fit a bigger breaker on the old cable, and do not use double adaptors.
A fire alarm or security panel is on its **own labelled circuit**, so it is not switched off by mistake with other loads.
A ceiling fan draws very little and can share a lighting circuit through its own control.

blocks.p: A 220 V fixed appliance is fed from **two line conductors** (plus a protective conductor, and a neutral only if the appliance needs 110 V for controls). It is switched and protected by a **two-pole breaker** that opens both lines at once. A single-pole breaker in one line only would leave the other line live when the appliance is 'off'; a fuse in the neutral, or an ordinary light switch, is no substitute.

Choose a breaker rated at or just above the appliance's current, of a type that suits the load, and **not above the maximum the maker allows (MOP)**. The cable must be able to carry what the breaker allows. A motor draws a large **starting (inrush) current** for a moment, so choose protection that will not trip on normal starting but still protects the cable; a separate overload device protects the motor. Never choose 'the smallest breaker that fits the board', and never leave a motor without overload protection.

A fixed appliance or machine has a **local isolator (disconnect switch)** near it, within sight, so the person servicing it can switch it off and lock it off where the work is done, without going back to a board that may be far away or locked. It also allows quick emergency switching off. Plan it **outside** wet areas, within reach, and not over hot plates or the appliance's moving parts.

head: Appliance
Isolator planning point
rows: Weatherproof, within sight of the unit, not blocking the maker's service clearances.
Weatherproof, rated above the pump's running current, close to the pump; an indoor light switch or a loose plug and outlet is not an isolator.
Within reach, but not above the hot plates.
Outside the bathroom, or out of reach of the water.

blocks.p: Plan GFCI (RCD) protection where the code the Centre uses asks: outlets near sinks, in bathrooms, kitchens, outdoors, garages and similar wet or damp places, and for equipment used outdoors. Ask the instructor which circuits the code edition in use requires it for; a GFCI is not needed on a doorbell transformer, or on the supply cable between the meter and the board.

A metal-cased appliance such as a stove needs a **protective (earth, equipment grounding) conductor** back to the board. Then a fault that makes the case live sends a large current through that conductor, the breaker trips quickly, and the case is no longer live. Without it the case can stay live, and the next person to touch it and a grounded object takes the shock. Double-insulated appliances (square-in-square symbol) are the exception and need no earth.

If the plan includes work in or at an existing board, the method statement must include **safe isolation**: switch off, lock off with your own padlock, tag, prove the tester on a proving unit, prove dead at the point of work between all conductors, and prove the tester again. Working quickly to keep the power off for less time is not a control; neither is simply switching off and starting. And **no work is ever done live**.

flow: Find the design current from the nameplate
Choose the breaker at or just above it, within the maker's maximum
Choose a cable whose **corrected** rating is at least the breaker's rating
Check the **volt drop**: mV/A/m × current × length ÷ 1 000, against the limit
If the drop is too high, use a larger cable
Check the choice against the maker's instructions

blocks.p: **Correction factors** lower a cable's table rating for heat, grouping and insulation. A cable in a hot roof space carries less current than the table says, so it is **derated** and may need to be larger. (Heat does not help current flow, and painting the cable white does not solve it.)

head: Check
Working
Result
rows: Volt drop: 30 m run, 10 A, 11 mV/A/m

ul: The **shortest safe route**, away from heat, hot pipes and damage.
Never loose across the floor or under a rug; never through the same sleeve as a gas pipe; keep clear of water pipes.
A longer route means more volt drop and more cable, and should not be chosen so that it 'can be moved later'.

head: Place
What to plan
rows: Outdoors (pump by a water tank, outdoor A/C)
Enclosures, isolators and glands with an **IP rating** for wet outdoor use; sun-resistant cable or conduit; rust-resistant fixings; GFCI protection.
Switches and controls outside the room or out of reach of the bath or shower; GFCI protection; equipment rated for damp.
Dedicated circuits for the stove and heavy appliances; outlets near sinks with GFCI protection; sealed fittings against steam and grease; cables kept away from the oven and hob heat.
Derate the cable; use equipment rated for the heat; keep recessed fittings clear of insulation or use a type rated for it.
Dust sheets, floor covers and a daily clean-up to protect the client's property.

blocks.note: Where an appliance is outdoors, an indoor-only isolator, a plastic indoor box or a switch 'hidden behind the tank' will fail. Plan equipment with an IP rating that suits the place, and check the rating on the item itself.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A **ceiling fan** is heavy and moves: it needs a fixing point rated for the fan's weight and movement, fixed to the structure (a fan-rated bracket or box on a rafter, beam or masonry anchor). A plastic box held up only by the supply cable, glue, or the light switch drop is not suitable.
A heavy **isolator** on a concrete block wall is fixed with wall plugs and screws sized for the load; nails in mortar joints, adhesive tape and cable ties round a pipe will not do.
Follow the maker's **clearances** around an outdoor A/C unit: they allow airflow, service access and safe working.
Fix equipment level and tight, and check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling.

**Spacing along a wall or ceiling line**: with n fittings evenly spaced and half a space at each end, the spacing is length ÷ n. Three spotlights on a 9 m wall: 9 ÷ 3 = 3.0 m apart, with the first 1.5 m from the end.
A **recessed fitting** in a ceiling with insulation must be rated for it, or kept clear: insulation packed round a hot lamp is a fire risk.
The highest-wattage lamp is not the right lamp: use the wattage the fitting is marked for.

head: Need
Why
rows: Lightning and switching surges destroy electronics.
A server rack should not share a circuit with a welder or a motor; their switching causes voltage dips and noise.
Never remove the earth to 'stop noise': it is needed for safety and for surge protection.
Static from hands can destroy the parts of a control board such as a gate motor's controller: touch earthed metal first, hold the board by its edges, use anti-static packaging.
Control wiring (inputs, outputs, low-voltage supplies) is not guessed.

sections.title: Planning the job: method, risk, order and coordination

blocks.p: List everything: the right breaker (a two-pole breaker, an isolator, cable and conduit for a 220 V split A/C unit; not a 6 A lighting breaker and lamp cord), fixings, glands, labels, tools, test instruments **with calibration in date**, PPE and access equipment.

The **method statement** is the written step-by-step plan of how the task will be done safely. It gives: the job details, the drawings and maker's instructions used; the people, their roles and competence; the tools, instruments and materials; the steps in order; the safety controls; the tests; and handover. It does **not** hold prices or payment schedules.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Safe isolation; no live work; insulated tools.
Drilling into hidden cables or water pipes
Check drawings; use a cable and pipe detector; drill small pilot holes.
Ladders or towers in good order, footed.
Manual handling of a motor or appliance
Dust mask, eye and ear protection; dust sheets.

blocks.p: The risk assessment says who could be harmed, the controls, and who is responsible. The method statement and risk assessment are signed and briefed to the team. The plan carries the approval of the **supervisor and, where needed, the client** before any fixing begins.

flow: Survey and mark out positions
Fix the appliance base, boxes, isolator and containment
Run the cable
Terminate at the appliance and the isolator
Inspect and test the circuit dead
Safe isolation at the board; connect the new circuit at the board **last**
The instructor or authorised person energises; live checks such as the GFCI test
Update the circuit chart and hand over

blocks.p: Why connect at the board last? The new circuit stays dead and isolated while it is being built, and is energised only after it has been inspected and tested. Run-the-cable, energise, then connect the appliance is the wrong order: it makes the cable live with open ends.

head: With
Agree
rows: Positions, timing, access, what will be disturbed, shutdowns.
Position of the indoor and outdoor units and the supply point for each.
Pipe routes, so cables stay clear of water and hot pipes.
Where the stove, fridge, microwave and hood go, so outlets are not hidden behind cabinets.
First fix before plastering; second fix after cabinets and the first coat.

blocks.p: Estimate the **labour hours** for each task: they set the programme (how many days) and the cost (hours × rate). Add materials, tools and test time, and get the plan approved.
Plan the checks that are done **dead**, before the supply is switched on, in this order:

flow: Visual inspection: cable, terminations, isolator, earth connection, labels
Continuity of the protective conductor, from the board end to the appliance's metal case (low-resistance ohmmeter)
Continuity of line and neutral conductors
Insulation resistance between conductors and to earth, to show there is no short and the insulation is sound
Polarity: breakers and switches in the line conductor
Record the results and compare them with the limits the specification or code gives

blocks.p: These are done dead after safe isolation because an insulation tester puts a high test voltage on the circuit and neither the instrument nor the person should be exposed to the supply. **Disconnect or remove sensitive electronic equipment and surge protectors** before an insulation resistance test, or the test voltage can damage them. Testing by touching terminals with a tester while live is not a test plan. Only after every test passes does the instructor, or on a real job the authorised person, energise the circuit and carry out live checks such as the GFCI trip test.

head: Item
Why
rows: So users and servicers follow the maker's advice for use and care.
So the client can claim if it fails.
They show the circuit was tested and give the next electrician something to compare.
So the new circuit can be found and isolated.
Showing the client the isolator, breaker and GFCI test
So the client can switch off in an emergency and check protection.
A record that the client has received the work and documents.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can say which document gives an appliance's supply, protection and clearances, and what the nameplate tells me.
I can survey the supply, board, route and position, and record what I find.
I can work out the current from power and voltage, and check the supply can carry the total.
I can explain why large loads use 220 V and have their own circuits.
I can choose between a single-pole and a two-pole breaker.
I can choose protection that suits a motor's starting current.
I can plan a local isolator and say why it is near the machine.
I can plan GFCI (RCD) protection and the earth conductor to a metal-cased appliance.
I can size a cable with correction factors and check the volt drop.
I can plan for outdoors, bathrooms, kitchens, hot roof spaces and the sea.
I can plan fixings, clearances, fan supports and recessed fittings.
I can plan for electronic equipment: surge protection, dedicated circuits and anti-static care.
I can write a method statement and risk assessment that include safe isolation.
I can put the work in order and coordinate with the other trades.
I can plan the dead tests in order and say who energises.
I can list the handover documents and why each is given.

terms: Circuit chart
The list in the board of every circuit, its breaker size and what it feeds.
Derating
Lowering a cable's current rating because of heat, grouping or insulation.
Isolator
A switch near an appliance so it can be switched off and locked off there.
IP rating
The code showing how well an enclosure keeps out dust and water.
Method statement
The written step-by-step plan of how a task will be done safely.
Nameplate
The plate on an appliance that gives its voltage, power and current.
Polarity
The correct connection of line, neutral and earth, with switches and breakers in the line.
Starting (inrush) current
The short burst of extra current a motor draws when it starts.
Surge protective device (SPD)
A device that protects equipment from voltage spikes.
Two-pole breaker
A breaker that opens both line conductors of a 220 V circuit together.
Volt drop
The voltage lost along a cable when current flows.
Wiring diagram
The maker's drawing of how an appliance's terminals and controls are connected.

c1.title: An instant shower heater in Old Harbour
c1.text: Mrs Williams in Old Harbour, St Catherine, has bought a 5.5 kW, 220 V instant shower heater for her bathroom. The house has a 110/220 V supply and a board with one spare way. The bathroom is at the back of the house, 18 m from the board along a route that crosses a hot, sunlit roof space. The installer's leaflet says the heater must have its own circuit with a switch outside the room.

c2.title: Ceiling fans in a church hall at Christiana
c2.text: A church hall at Christiana, Manchester, is to get four 110 V ceiling fans, each rated 75 W, evenly spaced along a ceiling line 10 m long, with half a space at each end. The ceiling is timber rafters under a zinc roof, and the carpenter has not yet closed the ceiling. The pastor wants the fans controlled from one wall plate.

c3.title: A restaurant kitchen in Falmouth
c3.text: A restaurant in Falmouth, Trelawny, is installing a 220 V, 8.8 kW oven, two 110 V commercial fridges of 1.1 kW each and an extractor hood. The kitchen is hot and steamy and the oven is to stand against a wall. The kitchen fitter's drawing shows the cabinets and the oven. The board has two spare ways.

c4.title: A pump at a Portmore car wash
c4.text: A car wash in Portmore, St Catherine, is adding a 220 V pump motor. The nameplate gives 7.5 A full-load current, and the starting current is several times that. The pump stands outdoors on a concrete pad, 40 m from the board, and the area is wet and splashed with soapy water. The cable is rated at 9.5 mV/A/m and the specification allows 3% volt drop on this circuit.

c5.title: A new clinic room in Black River
c5.text: A clinic in Black River, St Elizabeth, is adding a room with a 220 V autoclave and a small server with a surge protector on a separate circuit. Two trainees will carry out the wiring, and Mr Reid, the planner, is writing the test plan. The circuit for the server has surge protective devices fitted at the outlets, and the new circuits will be connected at the existing board.

questions.q: What current should the planner expect the 5.5 kW, 220 V shower heater to draw?
questions.why: Current = power ÷ voltage = 5 500 ÷ 220 = 25 A. Dividing by 110 V instead would give 50 A, a common error; the circuit is 220 V, so 25 A is correct.

questions.q: Which protection suits the heater's circuit?
o: A two-pole breaker of the maker's rating on its own circuit
A single-pole breaker shared with the bathroom light circuit
An ordinary light switch rated at 10 A
A fuse in the neutral conductor only
questions.why: A 220 V heater is fed from two line conductors, so a two-pole breaker opens both. Its large load needs its own circuit, and the breaker rating comes from the maker's instructions. A light switch or a neutral fuse protects nothing.

questions.q: Where should the heater's isolating switch be planned?
o: On the floor behind the toilet, out of sight
Inside the shower, where it is easy to reach
Beside the basin taps, at hand height
Outside the bathroom, away from water and wet hands
questions.why: Switches and controls in wet rooms are placed outside the room or out of reach of the water, so that wet hands never touch live parts. The maker's leaflet for this heater says the same.

questions.q: Part of the 18 m route crosses a hot roof space. What should the planner do about it?
o: Use a thinner cable, because heat helps current flow
Derate the cable for the heat and check the volt drop
Ignore the heat, as roof temperature does not affect cable
Paint the cable white to reflect the heat
questions.why: Heat lowers the current a cable can carry safely, so its table rating is multiplied by a correction factor and a larger cable may be needed. Then check the volt drop over the 18 m.

questions.q: How far from the end wall should the first of the four fans be?
questions.why: With four fans evenly spaced and half a space at each end, the spacing is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 m, and half of that, 1.25 m, is left at each end.

questions.q: What is the total current of the four 75 W fans at 110 V, and where can they be connected?
o: About 27 A, on a circuit of their own, with a large breaker
About 2.7 A, on a lighting circuit with their own control
About 0.7 A, on a 220 V circuit only, with its own switch
About 2.7 A, but only on the stove circuit, to avoid overload
questions.why: 4 × 75 = 300 W; 300 ÷ 110 = 2.7 A. That is small enough to share a lighting circuit through the fans' own control, as long as the maker's instructions and the circuit rating are respected.

questions.q: The fans will be hung from the timber rafters. What must the plan include?
o: A fan-rated bracket fixed to the roof structure
Plastic boxes held up by the supply cable
Strong glue between the fan and the zinc sheet
A hook fixed to the wall switch drop
questions.why: A fan is heavy and moves as it turns, so its support must be rated for its weight and movement and fixed to the structure. The supply cable, glue and a switch drop cannot carry it.

questions.q: When should the fan positions and their fixing points be agreed with the carpenter?
o: After the ceiling has been closed and painted
When the fans are first switched on
Before the ceiling is closed
When the pastor complains about a wobbling fan
questions.why: Fixing points must be in the structure before the ceiling hides it, so the planner marks the positions with the carpenter at the planning stage, and puts them on the drawing.

questions.q: What current does the 8.8 kW, 220 V oven draw?
questions.why: Current = 8 800 ÷ 220 = 40 A. It is a 220 V load and has its own two-pole breaker, so it is not divided by 110 V.

questions.q: Where should the oven's isolator be planned?
o: Directly over the hot plates, for convenience
On the extractor hood duct, close to the steam
Behind the oven, so that the cook cannot touch it
Within reach, but not above the hot parts of the oven
questions.why: The isolator must be reachable in an emergency, but heat and steam will damage it and burn a hand reaching for it. Plan it within reach, away from the hot surfaces and the cooking area.

questions.q: The cable's final connection to the oven passes close to hot metal. What should be planned?
o: Heat-rated cable or flex, kept clear of hot parts
Ordinary PVC cable, because the oven is off at night
A thinner cable, so that it heats up less in the kitchen
Any cable, if it is covered with a sleeve from a gas pipe
questions.why: Heat softens and damages ordinary insulation. The final connection uses a heat-rated cable or flex, as the maker's instructions say, and is routed so it never touches hot parts.

questions.q: The kitchen is hot and steamy. Which requirement should the plan add for its light fittings?
o: Plain indoor fittings, at the lowest height possible
Open fittings, so that the steam can escape
Sealed fittings that suit steam and grease
No fittings, with lighting from the dining room only
questions.why: Steam and grease get into open fittings, corroding the contacts and creating a shock and fire risk. Plan sealed fittings with a suitable IP rating, and keep cables away from the heat.

questions.q: What volt drop will the pump's 40 m cable have at full load, and is it acceptable?
o: About 0.29 V: so small that no check was needed
About 28.5 V: far over the 6.6 V limit, so not acceptable
About 2.9 V: over the 2.2 V limit, so not acceptable
About 2.9 V: under the 6.6 V limit, so acceptable
questions.why: Volt drop = 9.5 × 7.5 × 40 ÷ 1 000 = 2.85 V. The limit is 3% of 220 V = 6.6 V, so the cable passes. The motor's starting current causes a larger drop for a moment, which the designer also bears in mind.

questions.q: Which isolator is suitable for the outdoor, splashed pump?
o: An indoor light switch rated at 5 A
A weatherproof isolator rated above 7.5 A
A weatherproof isolator rated at 5 A
A plug and outlet left hanging beside the pump
questions.why: The isolator must have an IP rating for a wet, outdoor place, be rated for the motor's running current (7.5 A), and be within sight of the pump so it can be locked off there. An indoor switch or an under-rated device would fail.

questions.q: The plan puts the connection at the existing board as the last step. What is the reason?
o: JPS requires the board connection to be done before anything else
The board's breakers will not work until the motor is connected
The new circuit stays dead and isolated until it is tested
It saves time, since the cable is live while the pump is wired
questions.why: Connecting at the board last means the circuit cannot be energised while it is being built or before the tests are passed. The new circuit is made safe first, then connected after safe isolation at the board.

questions.q: Before the insulation resistance test on the server circuit, what should Mr Reid's plan say about the electronic equipment and surge protectors?
o: Disconnect or remove them: the test voltage can damage them
Leave them connected so that they are tested too
Switch them on to prove they work during the test
Tape over their terminals and test the circuit as normal
questions.why: An insulation tester applies a high voltage (often 250 or 500 V) that can damage electronics and surge protectors. They are disconnected or removed for the test, and checked separately as the maker says.

questions.q: Which dead test confirms that a fault in the autoclave's metal case would have a path to trip the breaker?
o: Polarity of the switches and breakers
Protective conductor continuity, board to case
Insulation resistance between line and neutral
A visual check of the paint round the autoclave
questions.why: Continuity of the protective conductor, measured with a low-resistance ohmmeter, shows an unbroken path from the board to the case, so a fault can draw the large current that trips the breaker.

questions.q: After the tests pass, what must be updated in the board before handover?
o: The firm's price list
The client's list of staff
The inspector's report on the old circuits
The circuit chart, showing the new circuits
questions.why: The circuit chart shows what each breaker feeds, so the new circuits can be found and isolated by the next person to work in the board. It is part of the handover documents.

questions.q: The maker's instructions ask for 300 mm clear space around an outdoor A/C unit, but the client wants it 100 mm from the wall to hide it. What should the planner do?
o: Fit it where the client asks, to keep the client happy
Fit it 100 mm from the wall and fit a larger breaker
Explain why, and agree a position within the clearances
Leave the clearance out, since the client has decided
questions.why: Clearances give the unit the airflow it needs and let people reach it safely for service. Follow the maker's instructions, explain why to the client, and offer another way to hide the unit that keeps the clearances.

questions.q: The test plan lists the instruments for the new circuit's dead tests. Which set is right?
o: Calibrated continuity and insulation testers, and a voltage tester
A multimeter left on its current range, and a lamp
A clamp meter and a non-contact voltage detector only
A thermal camera and a power logger for the week
questions.why: Dead testing needs a low-resistance continuity tester, an insulation tester, and a two-pole voltage tester with its proving unit for safe isolation, all in calibration. A clamp meter, a detector, a lamp, a thermal camera and a logger do not prove dead or test the circuit.
